```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 120)
```

```{r load}
for (f in c("R/db.R", "R/analysis.R", "R/plots.R")) source(f)
if (!file.exists("output/lob.sqlite")) stop("run `Rscript run_all.R` first")
con <- db_connect("output/lob.sqlite")
res <- analyze(con)
```

## Data

The data is a LOBSTER message file (every order submission, cancellation and
execution) paired with its order book file (the top levels of the book after
every message). This report covers `r data_description(res$info)`. Running
`run_all.R` with no arguments simulates a trading day instead, and the same
pipeline runs unchanged on either.

All of the microstructure measures are computed in SQL (`sql/`). R fits the
models and draws the charts.

```{r summary}
knitr::kable(res$summary, col.names = c("Metric", "Value"))
```

## 1. Spreads

```{r spreads}
plot_spread_distribution(res)
```

Quoted spread, weighted by time: **$`r sprintf('%.4f', res$quoted_spread)`**.
Effective spread (what traders actually pay, from trade prices against the
pre-trade mid): **$`r sprintf('%.4f', res$effective_spread)`**.
Roll's (1984) spread, inferred only from trade-price autocovariance:
**$`r sprintf('%.4f', res$roll)`**.

## 2. Queue imbalance and the next price move

$$\text{Imbalance} = \frac{Q^{bid} - Q^{ask}}{Q^{bid} + Q^{ask}}$$

When the bid queue is much larger than the ask queue, the ask is more likely
to be depleted first, so the next mid-price move is more likely to be up.

```{r imbalance}
plot_imbalance(res)
```

Every book state between two mid moves is waiting for the same move, so the
test uses one observation per move: the first state with a non-zero imbalance
after the previous move. On that basis the sign of L1 imbalance predicts the
next mid move **`r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * res$imbalance$hit_rate_l1)`** of the
time (n = `r format(res$imbalance$n, big.mark = ",")` moves). Counting every
book state would give `r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * res$imbalance$hit_rate_all_states)`,
but those states overlap, so that figure overstates the signal.

```{r imbalance-model}
summary(res$imbalance$model_l1)$coefficients
```

## 3. Order flow imbalance (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov 2014)

OFI nets out the changes in queue size at the best bid and ask on every book
update. Summed over 10-second buckets, it explains price changes linearly:

$$\Delta P_k = \beta \, \frac{OFI_k}{\bar D_k} + \varepsilon_k$$

```{r ofi}
plot_ofi(res)
summary(res$ofi$model_scaled)$coefficients
```

R² = **`r sprintf('%.3f', res$ofi$r2_scaled)`**, scaled by depth
(`r sprintf('%.3f', res$ofi$r2_raw)`, unscaled).

## 4. Price impact and transaction costs

```{r impact}
plot_impact(res)
```

Fitting $\text{impact} \propto \text{size}^{b}$ across trade-size buckets gives
$b$ = **`r sprintf('%.2f', res$impact$exponent)`** (95% CI
`r sprintf('%.2f', res$impact$ci[1])` to `r sprintf('%.2f', res$impact$ci[2])`,
from `r res$impact$n_buckets` size buckets), which is
`r impact_verdict(res$impact)`. The empirical "square-root law" predicts about
0.5. This is one day of one stock, fitted on bucket averages, so treat it as a
description of this sample and not a test of the law.

```{r costs}
plot_cost_decomposition(res)
knitr::kable(res$impact$by_size, digits = 3)
```

The effective spread splits into the **realized spread** (what the liquidity
provider keeps after 5 seconds) and **2 × price impact** (what they lose to
informed flow, i.e. adverse selection). Impact horizons are measured exactly:
the mid at a horizon is the last quote at or before the trade time plus that
horizon.

Some trades execute against hidden orders. LOBSTER reports their direction,
but many fill at the mid, where the price can't confirm it, so costs are
also split by whether a trade touched hidden liquidity:

```{r costs-hidden}
knitr::kable(res$costs_by_liquidity, digits = 3)
```

## 5. Volatility signature

```{r signature}
plot_signature(res)
```

If prices had no microstructure noise, realized volatility would be flat
across sampling intervals. Trade prices bounce between the bid and the ask,
which inflates realized volatility at 1–10 second sampling. Mid quotes are
much more robust. This is why high-frequency volatility estimators subsample
or use pre-averaging.

## 6. Trade-sign autocorrelation

```{r acf}
plot_sign_acf(res)
```

Buys tend to follow buys. Large parent orders get split into many child
orders (Lillo & Farmer 2004).

## 7. Intraday patterns

```{r intraday, fig.height = 6}
plot_intraday(res)
```

```{r close, include = FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

## References

- Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov (2014). *The Price Impact of Order Book Events.* Journal of Financial Econometrics.
- Cartea, Jaimungal & Penalva (2015). *Algorithmic and High-Frequency Trading.* Cambridge University Press.
- Roll (1984). *A Simple Implicit Measure of the Effective Bid-Ask Spread.* Journal of Finance.
- Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Labys (2000). *Great Realizations.* Risk.
- Lillo & Farmer (2004). *The Long Memory of the Efficient Market.* Studies in Nonlinear Dynamics & Econometrics.
- Gould & Bonart (2016). *Queue Imbalance as a One-Tick-Ahead Price Predictor in a Limit Order Book.* Market Microstructure and Liquidity.
